clinicalPearls: TTP results from a severe deficiency of the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease ADAMTS13, either acquired through an autoantibody or, rarely, congenital (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome).

The classic pentad of fever, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment and fluctuating neurological signs is seldom complete; unexplained microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia is sufficient to act.

The blood film is central to diagnosis, showing prominent schistocytes, thrombocytopenia and polychromasia, with a raised lactate dehydrogenase, raised unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin and a negative direct antiglobulin test.
Neurological features characteristically fluctuate and range from headache and confusion to seizures, focal deficits and coma, and may be transient.
TTP is a haematological emergency: plasma exchange should be started urgently on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result to return.
Platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless there is life-threatening haemorrhage, as it may aggravate microvascular thrombosis.
Standard adjuncts to plasma exchange in acquired TTP include corticosteroids, rituximab and the anti-von Willebrand factor agent caplacizumab.
The PLASMIC score aids estimation of the likelihood of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency while the confirmatory assay is awaited, and congenital TTP is managed with plasma infusion rather than exchange.
reference.pathophysiology: Deficient activity of ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers as they are released from endothelium, allows these hyperadhesive multimers to persist in the circulation. They spontaneously bind and aggregate platelets under high shear, generating platelet-rich microthrombi in the arterioles and capillaries of multiple organs, especially the brain, heart and kidneys. Passage of red cells across these partially occluded, fibrin- and platelet-laden vessels causes mechanical fragmentation and a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, while platelet consumption produces thrombocytopenia. In acquired disease an IgG autoantibody inhibits or clears ADAMTS13, whereas the congenital form is due to biallelic mutations in the ADAMTS13 gene. Unlike DIC, the coagulation cascade is not primarily activated, so the clotting screen is typically normal.
additionalDifferentials: haemolytic uraemic syndrome (including Shiga toxin-associated and complement-mediated forms)
additionalInvestigations: lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin
ADAMTS13 activity with anti-ADAMTS13 antibody or inhibitor assay
troponin and electrocardiogram to detect cardiac involvement
redFlags: any new or fluctuating neurological deficit, seizure or reduced consciousness
chest pain, arrhythmia or other evidence of cardiac involvement
a rapidly rising lactate dehydrogenase indicating ongoing microangiopathy
haemodynamic instability or evolving multi-organ dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Untreated TTP carries a very high mortality, but prompt plasma exchange with immunosuppression allows most patients to survive the acute episode. Acquired TTP is prone to relapse and warrants long-term monitoring of ADAMTS13 activity.
pitfalls: giving prophylactic platelet transfusions, which may worsen microthrombosis
delaying plasma exchange while awaiting the ADAMTS13 result
confusing TTP with DIC, forgetting that the coagulation screen is usually normal in TTP
overlooking subtle or transient neurological signs and clinically silent cardiac involvement
attributing the picture to sepsis or malignancy and missing a treatable thrombotic microangiopathy
references: British Society for Haematology guideline on the diagnosis and management of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and other thrombotic microangiopathies
International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis guidelines on TTP
management: Start plasma exchange urgently on clinical suspicion without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result, as it is the definitive mainstay of treatment
Give corticosteroid immunosuppression for acquired autoantibody-mediated disease
Add the anti-von Willebrand factor agent caplacizumab to reduce microthrombosis, with rituximab for refractory or relapsing immune disease
Manage congenital (Upshaw-Schulman) disease with plasma infusion or recombinant ADAMTS13 replacement
Avoid platelet transfusion unless there is life-threatening haemorrhage, since it may aggravate microvascular thrombosis
Provide supportive care with folate, red cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia and organ support for neurological or cardiac involvement
Monitor ADAMTS13 activity long term under haematology follow-up to detect and pre-empt relapse
